claim: The physical interactions of growing bacterial cells with each other and with their surroundings significantly affect the structure and dynamics of biofilms.
source: The physical interactions of growing bacterial cells with each other and with their surroundings significantly affect the structure and dynamics of biofilms.
evidence: This is a general statement in the abstract that sets up the context for the study.

claim: A 3D agent-based model was formulated to describe the establishment of simple bacterial colonies expanding by the physical force of their growth.
source: Here a 3D agent-based model is formulated to describe the establishment of simple bacterial colonies expanding by the physical force of their growth.
evidence: The abstract describes the development of the model as a primary contribution of the work.

claim: The model captures key dynamical features of colony growth by non-motile, non EPS-producing E. coli cells on hard agar with a single set of parameters.
source: With a single set of parameters, the model captures key dynamical features of colony growth by non-motile, non EPS-producing E. coli cells on hard agar.
evidence: The abstract states that the model successfully reproduces experimental observations using a single parameter set.

claim: Radial colony expansion is not limited by nutrients as commonly believed, but by mechanical forces.
source: The model, supported by experiment on colony growth in different types and concentrations of nutrients, suggests that radial colony expansion is not limited by nutrients as commonly believed, but by mechanical forces.
evidence: The abstract presents this as a key finding supported by both model and experiment.

claim: Nutrient penetration governs vertical colony growth through thin layers of vertically oriented cells lifting up their ancestors from the bottom.
source: Nutrient penetration instead governs vertical colony growth, through thin layers of vertically oriented cells lifting up their ancestors from the bottom.
evidence: The abstract states this as a finding from the model regarding vertical growth mechanism.

claim: Bacteria often form dense biofilms with complex spatiotemporal structures.
source: Bacteria often form dense biofilms with complex spatiotemporal structures (Costerton et al., 1995; Nadell et al., 2016; O'Toole et al., 2000; Stoodley et al., 2002).
evidence: This statement is supported by multiple citations to prior literature.

claim: Mechanical and biochemical interactions, together with cell growth, motility, and signaling, are common elements underlying the rich variety of patterns and behaviors observed in biofilms.
source: Mechanical and biochemical interactions, together with cell growth, motility, and signaling, are some of the common elements underlying the rich variety of patterns and behaviors observed.
evidence: This is a general statement about biofilm formation based on established knowledge.

claim: Biofilms often play important roles in diverse settings ranging from environment to human health.
source: Biofilms often play important roles in diverse settings ranging from environment to human health (Costerton et al., 1999; Jayaraman and Wood, 2008; Potera, 1999).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Biofilms are notoriously difficult to study experimentally because of their opaqueness, high heterogeneity and complex organization, involving multiple spatial and temporal scales.
source: But they are notoriously difficult to study experimentally because of their opaqueness, high heterogeneity and complex organization, involving multiple spatial and temporal scales (Roberts et al., 2015; Stewart and Franklin, 2008).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Biofilm-bound bacteria alter their micro-environment by secreting various polysaccharides, forming heterogeneous matrices of filaments that bind cells together within biofilms.
source: In addition, biofilm-bound bacteria alter their micro-environment by secreting various polysaccharides, forming heterogeneous matrices of filaments that bind cells together within biofilms (Branda et al., 2005; Flemming and Wingender, 2010).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Various computational models have been constructed to capture different aspects of biofilm development.
source: Over the years, various computational models have been constructed to capture different aspects of biofilm development (Alpkvist et al., 2006; Espeso et al., 2015; Ginovart et al., 2002; Klapper and Dockery, 2002; Kreft et al., 2001; Kreft et al., 1998; Picioreanu et al., 2004; Seminara et al., 2012; Tierra et al., 2015).
evidence: This statement is supported by multiple citations to prior modeling literature.

claim: Most biofilm models are 'descriptive' in nature and the complexity of the biofilms makes it difficult to make quantitative comparison between experimental data and model predictions.
source: However, most of these models are 'descriptive' in nature – the complexity of the biofilms makes it difficult to make quantitative comparison between experimental data and model predictions.
evidence: This is a critical assessment of prior modeling work.

claim: The simplest version of biofilm is the growth of a simple bacterial colony on hard agar surface, with cells pushing against each other by the force of their own physical growth, without motility and without extracellular polysaccharides.
source: The simplest among these is the growth of a simple bacterial colony on hard agar surface, with cells pushing against each other by the force of their own physical growth, without motility and without extracellular polysaccharides (Boyer et al., 2011; Cole et al., 2015; Farrell et al., 2013; Ghosh et al., 2015; Grant et al., 2014; Jayathilake et al., 2017; Rudge et al., 2013; Rudge et al., 2012; Volfson et al., 2008)
evidence: This statement is supported by multiple citations to prior literature.

claim: The growth of simple bacterial colonies has been increasingly used in recent years as a model of microbial range expansion in studies of population genetics and ecology.
source: In addition to serving as simpler models of biofilms, the growth of such colonies has been increasingly used in recent years as a model of microbial range expansion in studies of population genetics and ecology (Hallatschek et al., 2007; Hallatschek and Nelson, 2010; Korolev et al., 2012).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: The growth of simple colonies has been investigated experimentally many decades ago.
source: Although the growth of such simple colonies has been investigated experimentally many decades ago (Cooper et al., 1968; Lewis and Wimpenny, 1981; Mitchell and Wimpenny, 1997; Palumbo et al., 1971; Pirt, 1967; Reyrolle and Letellier, 1979; Wimpenny, 1979), surprisingly, there has not yet been a common quantitative understanding of the basic elements controlling their growth, for example what factors determine the radial and vertical expansion speeds.
evidence: This statement is supported by multiple citations to historical literature.

claim: There has not yet been a common quantitative understanding of the basic elements controlling colony growth, for example what factors determine the radial and vertical expansion speeds.
source: Although the growth of such simple colonies has been investigated experimentally many decades ago (Cooper et al., 1968; Lewis and Wimpenny, 1981; Mitchell and Wimpenny, 1997; Palumbo et al., 1971; Pirt, 1967; Reyrolle and Letellier, 1979; Wimpenny, 1979), surprisingly, there has not yet been a common quantitative understanding of the basic elements controlling their growth, for example what factors determine the radial and vertical expansion speeds.
evidence: This is an assessment of the state of the field that motivates the current study.

claim: The model incorporates elements of nutrient diffusion, cell-cell and cell-agar mechanical interactions, and a unique cell-level model of surface tension.
source: In this study, we develop a conceptually simple, yet physically realistic three-dimensional computational model, incorporating the elements of nutrient diffusion, cell-cell and cell-agar mechanical interactions, and introducing a unique cell-level model of surface tension.
evidence: This describes the key components of the model developed in the study.

claim: The model is efficiently implemented with a parallel algorithm, enabling the simulation of a colony comprising a few million cells within 24 hr.
source: Our model is efficiently implemented with a parallel algorithm, enabling the simulation of a colony comprising a few million cells within 24 hr.
evidence: This describes the computational efficiency of the model implementation.

claim: The model is able to capture many observed features of the growing colonies, including the conic shape, the linear growth of the colony radius and height, and their dependence on the cell growth rate.
source: The model is able to capture many observed features of the growing colonies, including the conic shape, the linear growth of the colony radius and height, and their dependence on the cell growth rate.
evidence: This describes the model's ability to reproduce experimental observations.

claim: Experiments were performed using E. coli K12 strain EQ59, which is non-motile and harbors constitutive GFP expression.
source: Experiments were performed using E. coli K12 strain EQ59, which is non-motile and harbors constitutive GFP expression; see 'Experimental Methods'.
evidence: This describes the experimental strain used in the study.

claim: Each colony was inoculated as a single cell from batch culture growing in mid-log phase on 1.5% (w/v) agar with glucose minimal media, and incubated, covered, at 37°C for up to 1.5 days.
source: Each colony was inoculated as a single cell from batch culture growing in mid-log phase on 1.5% (w/v) agar with glucose minimal media, and incubated, covered, at 37°C for up to 1.5 days.
evidence: This describes the experimental protocol for colony growth.

claim: Starting with a single cell, the colony remained a single layer through the first 13 hours.
source: Starting with a single cell, the colony remained a single layer through the first 13 hours (Figure 1AB)
evidence: This is an experimental observation supported by confocal microscopy data shown in Figure 1.

claim: The colony developed into a 3D colony over time, maintaining an approximate conic shape through the ensuing 10-15 hours after buckling.
source: It then developed into a 3D colony over time, maintaining an approximate conic shape through the ensuing 10-15 hours after buckling (Figure 1G).
evidence: This is an experimental observation supported by confocal microscopy data shown in Figure 1.

claim: As the colony grew further beyond t=24h, the gain in height slowed down while radial expansion continued at the same speed.
source: As the colony grew further, the gain in height slowed down while radial expansion continued at the same speed (Figure 1H and Figure 1—figure supplement 1), leading to a significant flattening of colony morphology.
evidence: This is an experimental observation supported by data shown in Figure 1H and Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: The findings of vertical linear growth disagree with earlier finding by Pirt.
source: Our findings of vertical linear growth disagree with earlier finding by Pirt (Pirt, 1967) which was first questioned by Wimpenny (Lewis and Wimpenny, 1981; Wimpenny, 1979).
evidence: This compares the current findings to prior literature.

claim: Earlier studies by Wimpenny reported much larger radial expansion speeds than the current study, suggesting that their study might be in a very different regime dominated by swarming motility.
source: However, the latter reported much larger radial expansion speeds than ours, suggesting that their study might be in a very different regime dominated by swarming motility (Wu et al., 2011).
evidence: This is an inference comparing the current results to prior literature.

claim: The number of cells in a colony increases exponentially for approximately 10 hours before it slows down.
source: From Figure 3A, we see that the number of cells in a colony increases exponentially for approximately 10 hours before it slows down.
evidence: This is a simulation result shown in Figure 3A.

claim: The model generates a constant width for the single-layer annulus region at the periphery, recapitulating report of a constant monolayer region by earlier mechanical study.
source: In particular, the model generates a constant width for the single-layer annulus region at the periphery, recapitulating report of a constant monolayer region by earlier mechanical study (Su et al., 2012).
evidence: This is a simulation result that is compared to prior literature.

claim: The model captures the linear increase of both the colony radius and height observed experimentally.
source: Thus, our model captures the linear increase of both the colony radius and height observed experimentally (Figure 1H).
evidence: This compares simulation results to experimental observations.

claim: The lower numerical values of the speeds obtained from simulations are due to parameter settings chosen to limit computational time.
source: The lower numerical values of the speeds obtained from simulations are due to parameter settings chosen to limit computational time; this will be discussed in 'Parameter dependence'.
evidence: This explains the discrepancy between simulation and experimental values.

claim: Cells near the top surface are oriented parallel to the colony surface, while cells away from the top surface are mostly oriented vertically.
source: The model shows that cells near the top surface are oriented parallel to the colony surface (shown in cyan), while cells away from the top surface are mostly oriented vertically (shown in yellow).
evidence: This is a simulation result shown in Figure 4A.

claim: The prediction of cell orientation at the top surface is validated by confocal scan of the colony in experiment.
source: This prediction is validated by confocal scan of the colony in experiment as shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1B.
evidence: This compares simulation predictions to experimental observations.

claim: The model shows a thin region at the periphery of the colony in which all cells are oriented in plane.
source: The model shows a thin region at the periphery of the colony in which all cells are oriented in plane.
evidence: This is a simulation result describing cell orientation at the periphery.

claim: Away from the periphery into the colony interior, more and more cells stand up vertically.
source: Away from the periphery into the colony interior, more and more cells stand up vertically.
evidence: This is a simulation result shown in Figure 4B.

claim: Appreciable fraction of cells (50%) picked up vertical orientation only when the radius reached 250 µm.
source: However, the internal verticalization took some time to develop (Figure 4—figure supplement 2); appreciable fraction of cells (50%) picked up vertical orientation only when the radius reached 250 µm.
evidence: This is a simulation result shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2.

claim: The velocity field points in the vertical direction throughout most of the colony, even at the top surface where cells are oriented parallel to the colony surface.
source: The velocity field points in the vertical direction throughout most of the colony, even at the top surface where cells are oriented parallel to the colony surface according to Figure 4C.
evidence: This is a simulation result shown in Figure 4D.

claim: Very close to the periphery in the bottom layer, the velocity field turns sideway and is oriented planarly.
source: Very close to the periphery in the bottom layer, the velocity field turns sideway; it is oriented planarly there and will be discussed below in the context of radial growth.
evidence: This is a simulation result shown in Figure 4D.

claim: Cells at the bottom of the colony are all young, indicating that the bottom layer is constantly dividing.
source: We see that cells at the bottom of the colony are all young (red), indicating that the bottom layer is constantly dividing.
evidence: This is a simulation result shown in Figure 4F.

claim: The oldest cells occupy the top/center region of the colony, and the next oldest age groups are located in different layers below the purple top region.
source: In contrast, the oldest cells (purple) occupy the top/center region of the colony, and the next oldest age groups (blue, green, etc.) are located in different layers below the purple top region.
evidence: This is a simulation result shown in Figure 4F.

claim: The cells are oriented vertically (except those close to the surface) and are pushed up by growing cells located within a 10 µm thick growth zone at the bottom; they stop dividing once pushed out of the growth zone.
source: Together, the above results suggest a simple picture of the vertical colony growth: The cells are oriented vertically (except those close to the surface) and are pushed up by growing cells located within a 10 µm thick growth zone at the bottom; they stop dividing once pushed out of the growth zone.
evidence: This is an inference from multiple simulation results.

claim: A disc-shaped growth zone at the bottom of the colony is intuitive, since cells at the bottom of the colony are in direct contact with the agar and hence have the best access to the nutrients.
source: This disc-shaped growth zone at the bottom of the colony may be intuitive, since cells at the bottom of the colony are in direct contact with the agar and hence have the best access to the nutrients.
evidence: This is a logical inference about nutrient access.

claim: The stationary nutrient profile drops quadratically at small heights (close to the agar surface), and exponentially at larger heights (top of the colony).
source: As shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1 and Appendix A2.3, this stationary profile drops quadratically at small heights (i.e. close to the agar surface), and exponentially at larger heights (top of the colony)
evidence: This is a simulation result shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1 and derived analytically in Appendix A2.3.

claim: The overall scale of the vertical ascending speed is 2-fold smaller in the simulation compared to experiment, attributed to the smaller nutrient concentrations used in the model.
source: Note that the overall scale of the vertical ascending speed is 2-fold smaller in the simulation. This is attributed to the smaller nutrient concentrations used in the model compared to experiment, as will be discussed further below in the section of parameter dependence.
evidence: This explains the discrepancy between simulation and experimental values.

claim: The periphery is largely comprised of horizontally oriented cells while the interior of the bottom layer has cells already oriented vertically.
source: The periphery is seen to be largely cyan while the interior is more yellowish, suggesting that cells at the interior of the bottom layer are already oriented vertically, consistent with the cross-sectional view shown in Figure 4A.
evidence: This is a simulation result shown in Figure 6A.

claim: Interior to the annulus, the in-plane projection of the director field vanishes, confirming that cells are largely oriented vertically.
source: Interior to the annulus, the in-plane projection of the director field vanishes, confirming that they are largely oriented vertically.
evidence: This is a simulation result shown in Figure 6B.

claim: There is a narrow annulus of non-vanishing velocity field at the outermost edge pointing radially outward.
source: We observe a narrow annulus of non-vanishing velocity field (arrows with finite length) at the outermost edge pointing radially outward; see also the side view provided in Figure 4D.
evidence: This is a simulation result shown in Figure 6C.

claim: Since the in-plane component of velocity vanishes inside the annulus, the driving force for radial colony expansion resides solely in the narrow annulus where cells are oriented planarly.
source: Since the in-plane component of velocity vanishes inside the annulus (turning to vertical speed as shown already in Figure 4D), the driving force for radial colony expansion reside solely in the narrow annulus where cells are oriented planarly (Figure 6B).
evidence: This is an inference from the simulation results.

claim: The width of the annulus determines the colony's radial expansion speed.
source: Just as the thickness of the growth zone determines the vertical ascension speed, here the width of the annulus determines the colony's radial expansion speed.
evidence: This is an inference from the simulation results.

claim: Where pressure is high, cells are oriented vertically and move vertically.
source: Where pressure is high, cells are oriented vertically and move vertically.
evidence: This is an inference from the simulation results.

claim: Increased pressure due to the physical growth of cells, which itself results from friction exerted by the substrate on the expanding cells, eventually forces cells to buckle and flow upward, manifested by the reorientation of cell directors in the vertical direction.
source: This analysis thus suggests that increased pressure due to the physical growth of cells, which itself results from friction exerted by the substrate on the expanding cells, eventually forces cells to buckle and flow upward, manifested by the reorientation of cell directors in the vertical direction.
evidence: This is an inference from the simulation results.

claim: Once the flow turns upward, pressure does not build up further due to the lack of friction with the agar surface.
source: Once the flow turns upward, pressure does not build up further due to the lack of friction with the agar surface.
evidence: This is an inference from the simulation results.

claim: Since the upward flow is resisted by the surface tension, pressure maxes out at a level that is mostly determined by the surface tension.
source: Since the upward flow is resisted by the surface tension, we conclude that pressure maxes out in this case at a level that is mostly determined by the surface tension.
evidence: This is an inference from the simulation results.

claim: At the colony periphery, nutrient concentration is close to the bulk level.
source: In fact, at the colony periphery, nutrient concentration is close to the bulk level (Figure 7D).
evidence: This is a simulation result shown in Figure 7D.

claim: At the inner edge of the monolayer region, pressure reaches a critical value that surface tension can no longer hold cells in a single layer, leading to buckling into the vertical dimension.
source: At the inner edge of the monolayer region, pressure reaches a critical value that surface tension can no longer hold cells in a single layer. There, some cells buckle into the vertical dimension, leading to vertical flow of cells and forming multiple layers (Figure 8—figure supplement 2), alleviating the further build-up of pressure.
evidence: This is an inference from the simulation results shown in Figure 8D and Figure 8—figure supplement 2.

claim: Experimental tests by varying the glucose concentration used in the agar show changes in line with the model predictions.
source: These predictions are further tested experimentally, by varying the glucose concentraton used in the agar (Figure 9C), and by repeating experiments in reduced agar densities (Figure 9D) which we expect to reduce the cell-agar friction. The observed changes are very much in line with the expectations of the model shown in Figure 9AB.
evidence: This is experimental data shown in Figure 9C and 9D that validates model predictions.

claim: Radial growth of the colony is not limited by nutrients while the vertical growth is limited by nutrients.
source: These results serve to validate the very important qualitative results of our study, that radial grow of the colony is not limited by nutrients while the vertial growth is limited by nutrients.
evidence: This is a key conclusion from the combined simulation and experimental results.

claim: The experimental range of expansion speeds could be obtained simply by adjusting the combinations of parameters.
source: The results of Figure 9AB show that the experimental range could be obtained simply by adjusting the combinations of parameters.
evidence: This is an inference from the parameter sensitivity analysis shown in Figure 9AB.

claim: Lower cell-agar friction would lead to colony spreading too rapidly in the radial direction, thus requiring larger simulation sizes and hence longer computational time.
source: Similarly, lower cell-agar friction would lead to colony spreading too rapidly in the radial diretion, thus requiring larger simulation sizes and hence again longer computational time.
evidence: This explains the choice of parameters used in the simulations.

claim: The growth zone is predicted to be disc-like and extended throughout the bottom of the colony, contrary to common belief.
source: The growth zone is predicted to be disc-like and extended throughout the bottom of the colony, contrary to common belief (see below).
evidence: This is a key prediction from the model shown in Figure 10.

claim: Radial growth is driven by cells at the outer perimeter of the growth zone; these cells are predicted to form a thin layer, oriented parallel to the agar due to the downward pull of surface tension.
source: Radial growth is driven by cells at the outer perimeter of the growth zone; these cells are predicted to form a thin layer, oriented parallel to the agar due to the downward pull of surface tension, with the width of the region determined by the onset of the buckling transition (which occurs when radial compression due to cell-agar friction overwhelms the surface tension).
evidence: This is a key prediction from the model shown in Figure 10.

claim: In the colony interior, cells are predicted to orient vertically and are mainly pushed upward by elongating cells in the bottom growth zone.
source: In the colony interior, cells are predicted to orient vertically and are mainly pushed upward by elongating cells in the bottom growth zone.
evidence: This is a key prediction from the model shown in Figure 10.

claim: Capturing all these behaviors within a single model and with a fixed set of parameters is a non-trivial task despite the seeming simplicity of this problem.
source: Capturing all these behaviors within a single model and with a fixed set of parameters is a non-trivial task despite the seeming simplicity of this problem.
evidence: This is an assessment of the modeling achievement.

claim: Many aspects of the model are taken from what are commonly adopted in the extensive literature devoted to this class of problems over the past decade.
source: Many aspects of our model are taken from what are commonly adopted in the extensive literature devoted to this class of problems over the past decade (Boyer et al., 2011; Cole et al., 2015; Farrell et al., 2013; Ghosh et al., 2015; Grant et al., 2014; Jayathilake et al., 2017; Rudge et al., 2013; Rudge et al., 2012; Volfson et al., 2008)
evidence: This acknowledges the use of established modeling approaches with citations.

claim: Unique to this study is the treatment of mechanical interactions, specifically friction and cell-level surface tension, which are at the root of all behaviors described.
source: Unique to our study is the treatment of mechanical interactions, specifically friction and cell-level surface tension, which we believe are at the root of all behaviors described above, including the forms of radial and vertical colony growth.
evidence: This highlights the novel contribution of the study.

claim: A key result of this study is that the linear radial growth is driven by the growth of a thin layer of radially oriented cells located at the colony periphery, whose width is determined by mechanical buckling.
source: A key result of our study is that the linear radial growth is driven by the growth of a thin layer of radially oriented cells located at the colony periphery, whose width is determined by mechanical buckling.
evidence: This is a key finding from the model.

claim: For a long time, linear radial expansion of bacterial colonies was attributed to a ring-shaped growth zone at the outer colony periphery due to nutrient diffusion.
source: Although the linear radial expansion of bacterial colonies has been known for about 50 years (Pirt, 1967), for a long time this was attributed to a ring-shaped growth zone at the outer colony periphery due to nutrient diffusion (Lewis and Wimpenny, 1981; Pirt, 1967; Wimpenny, 1979).
evidence: This describes the historical understanding with citations.

claim: Only quite recently has the notion been made that mechanical effects might also lead to linear radial growth.
source: Only quite recently has the notion been made that mechanical effects might also lead to linear radial growth (Farrell et al., 2013; Su et al., 2012).
evidence: This describes recent developments in the field with citations.

claim: Su et al. (2012) showed experimental results that implicated the interplay of forces in the radial expansion of colonies.
source: (Su et al., 2012) showed experimental results that implicated the interplay of forces in the radial expansion of colonies.
evidence: This cites prior experimental work.

claim: Farrell et al. (2013) proposed mechanical effects as a colloquial rationalization of numerical results generated by toy models with unrealistic details, for example a 'gravity-like' adhesion force acting on all cells in the colony.
source: (Farrell et al., 2013) proposed mechanical effects as a colloquial rationalization of numerical results generated by toy models with unrealistic details, for example a 'gravity-like' adhesion force acting on all cells in the colony.
evidence: This cites and critiques prior modeling work.

claim: In this study, the adhesion of cells to the agar surface is provided by the surface tension of the liquid surrounding cells in the colony.
source: In our study, the adhesion of cells to the agar surface is provided by the surface tension of the liquid surrounding cells in the colony.
evidence: This describes a key feature of the model.

claim: A novel cell-level model of surface tension is introduced which acts only on cells at the colony surface, distinct from common models of surface tension which depends on the macroscopic curvature of the colony surface and cannot describe thin layers.
source: We introduce a novel cell-level model of surface tension which acts only on cells at the colony surface, distinct from common models of surface tension which depends on the macroscopic curvature of the colony surface and cannot describe thin layers.
evidence: This describes a novel contribution of the model.

claim: This unique surface tension model enables capturing the dynamics from the initial single-layer cell growth, through buckling, to the growth of a macroscopic colony.
source: It is this unique surface tension model that enables us to capture the dynamics from the initial single-layer cell growth, through buckling, to the growth of a macroscopic colony.
evidence: This describes the importance of the novel surface tension model.

claim: This cell-level surface tension, responsible for pressing cells into the agar thereby generating friction that eventually causes buckling, cell reorientation and vertical colony growth, is the source of all mechanical interactions in the colony.
source: This cell-level surface tension, responsible for pressing cells into the agar thereby generating friction that eventually causes buckling, cell reorientation and vertical colony growth, is thus the source of all mechanical interactions in the colony.
evidence: This describes the role of surface tension in the model.

claim: A strong, uniform force such as the ones used in Farrell et al. (2013) would lead to artificially flattened colonies, especially at the colony center where the height is the highest, since the force is proportional to the height in that model.
source: A strong, uniform force such as the ones used in (Farrell et al., 2013) would lead to artificially flattened colonies, especially at the colony center where the height is the highest, since the force is proportional to the height in that model.
evidence: This critiques a prior modeling approach with citation.

claim: The characterization of colony growth for different nutrients (which give rise to different cell growth rates) is regarded as a unique contribution by this study.
source: We regard the characterization of colony growth for different nutrients (which give rise to different cell growth rates) as a unique contribution by our study.
evidence: This highlights a unique contribution of the study.

claim: The knowledge of the dependence of colony growth on cell growth allows discrimination of different models of colony growth.
source: The knowledge of the dependence of colony growth on cell growth allows us to discriminate different models of colony growth.
evidence: This describes the utility of the growth rate dependence analysis.

claim: Viscous drag (i.e., friction proportional to the velocity difference) is the form adopted in most models of cell dynamics.
source: Viscous drag (i.e., friction proportional to the velocity difference) is the form adopted in most models of cell dynamics (Farrell et al., 2013; Ghosh et al., 2015; Rudge et al., 2012).
evidence: This describes common practice in the field with citations.

claim: This study adopts a form of friction commonly used in modeling granular solids, involving a static friction depending on relative velocity, capped by a dynamic friction which is independent of the velocity.
source: We instead adopt a form commonly used in modeling granular solids (Brilliantov et al., 1996; Cundall and Strack, 1979; Kuwabara and Kono, 1987; Shäfer et al., 1996). It involves a static friction depending on relative velocity, capped by a dynamic friction which is independent of the velocity.
evidence: This describes the friction model used with citations.

claim: This form of friction was introduced in one of the first models of 2D colony growth.
source: This form, introduced in one of the first models of 2D colony growth (Volfson et al., 2008), exerts a pressure which is independent of the speed of radial expansion, leading to a growth rate-independent buckling width and hence a radial expansion speed that is proportional to cell growth rate, in agreement with our experiments.
evidence: This cites the origin of the friction model and describes its properties.

claim: A model based on static friction would have the buckling width reducing with increasing cell growth rate, giving a sublinear dependence of radial expansion speed on cell growth rate which is not compatible with the experimental data.
source: In contrast, a model based on static friction would have the buckling width reducing with increasing cell growth rate, giving a sublinear dependence of radial expansion speed on cell growth rate which is not compatible with the data in Figure 1I.
evidence: This is a prediction that is tested against experimental data.

claim: In a model with static friction alone, a much weaker growth-rate dependence of radial expansion speed was obtained.
source: Indeed, in a model with static friction alone, a much weaker growth-rate dependence of radial expansion speed was obtained (Figure 8F blue triangles).
evidence: This is a simulation result shown in Figure 8F.

claim: Fisher-Kolmogorov (FK) dynamics has been used as a phenomenological model to describe radial colony expansion, and has been successful in describing certain spatial patterns formed in growing colonies.
source: Along a different line, Fisher-Kolmogorov (FK) dynamics has been used as a phenomenological model to describe radial colony expansion, and has been successful in describing certain spatial patterns formed in growing colonies (Cao et al., 2016).
evidence: This cites an alternative modeling approach.

claim: FK dynamics would predict a square-root dependence of the radial expansion speed on the cell growth rate, which will need to be reformulated to conform to the observed dependences.
source: However, FK dynamics would predict a square-root dependence of the radial expansion speed on the cell growth rate (Fisher, 1937; Kolmogorov et al., 1937), which will need to be reformulated to conform to the observed dependences.
evidence: This critiques an alternative modeling approach with citations.

claim: The linear vertical growth of the colony is dissected for the first time qualitatively here since it was first reported.
source: In addition to the well-known linear radial growth, the linear vertical growth of the colony is dissected for the first time qualitatively here since it was first reported (Lewis and Wimpenny, 1981; Wimpenny, 1979).
evidence: This highlights a novel contribution with citations to prior reports.

claim: The analysis shows that the vertical expansion speed is limited by the depth that nutrient can penetrate upward into the colony from the agar.
source: Our analysis shows that the vertical expansion speed is limited by the depth that nutrient can penetrate upward into the colony from the agar.
evidence: This is a key finding from the model analysis.

claim: Accompanying the result of vertical growth is the predicted vertical orientation of cells in the colony interior, which transitions from the radial orientation at the outer periphery.
source: Accompanying our result of vertical growth is the predicted vertical orientation of cells in the colony interior, which transitions from the radial orientation at the outer periphery (i.e., the monolayer zone colored in cyan in Figure 10).
evidence: This is a prediction from the model shown in Figure 10.

claim: Cell verticalization has been observed experimentally for Vibrio parahaemolyticus and for Vibrio Cholerae.
source: Cell verticalization has been observed experimentally for Vibrio parahaemolyticus (Enos-Berlage and McCarter, 2000) and for Vibrio Cholerae (Beroz et al., 2018; Yan et al., 2016).
evidence: This cites prior experimental observations.

claim: In both Vibrio cases, vertical orientations could be seen already for very small bacterial colonies, possibly due to their production of extracellular polysaccharide substance (EPS).
source: In both cases, vertical orientations could be seen already for very small bacterial colonies, possibly due to their production of extracellular polysaccharide substance (EPS).
evidence: This is an inference about prior experimental observations.

claim: In this work, verticalization is predicted to occur for plain bacterial colonies as well, without the need of any EPS, but at much larger colony sizes.
source: In this work, verticalization is predicted to occur for plain bacterial colonies as well, without the need of any EPS, but at much larger colony sizes.
evidence: This is a prediction from the model.

claim: Verticalization has not been observed directly for the colonies in this study due to multiple scattering associated with very dense colonies.
source: We have not been able to observe verticalization directly for our colonies due to multiple scattering associated with very dense colonies we are studying. This is left as a challenge for future studies.
evidence: This acknowledges a limitation of the experimental observations.

claim: In this model, verticalization results from an interplay among colony surface tension, cell-agar friction and the physical force of expansion due to cell growth.
source: In our model, verticalization results from an interplay among colony surface tension, cell-agar friction and the physical force of expansion due to cell growth.
evidence: This describes the mechanism of verticalization in the model.

claim: Beroz et al. (2018) also introduced a discrete model to describe cell verticalization, where verticalization resulted from a similar mechanical instability due to the interplay between in-plane compression force and cell-agar adhesion.
source: (Beroz et al., 2018) also introduced a discrete model to describe cell verticalization. In their model, verticalization resulted from a similar mechanical instability due to the interplay between in-plane compression force and cell-agar adhesion.
evidence: This cites and describes a related modeling study.

claim: Generally, the radial expansion speed is expected to be controlled by the buckling width and vertical expansion speed to be controlled by the thickness of the growth zone.
source: Generally, we expect the radial expansion speed to be controlled by the buckling width and vertical expansion speed be controlled by the thickness of the growth zone.
evidence: This is a general prediction from the model.

claim: If agar hardness or ambient humidity is changed, the effect on air-liquid surface tension is expected to affect the buckling width and the ratio of the radial and vertical expansion speeds, hence changing the colony aspect ratio.
source: Thus, if agar hardness or ambient humidity is changed, the effect on air-liquid surface tension is expected to affect the buckling width and the ratio of the radial and vertical expansion speeds, hence changing the colony aspect ratio.
evidence: This is a prediction from the model.

claim: During later stages of colony growth when oxygen becomes limiting in the colony interior, the obligatory excretion of large amounts of fermentation product associated with anaerobiosis is predicted to lower the pH in colony interior and thereby slow down vertical colony growth while not affecting the radial growth.
source: Also, during later stages of colony growth when oxygen becomes limiting in the colony interior, the obligatory excretion of large amounts of fermentation product associated with anaerobiosis is predicted to lower the pH in colony interior and thereby slow down vertical colony growth while not affecting the radial growth.
evidence: This is a prediction from the model.

claim: Observations shown in Figure 1H and Figure 1—figure supplement 1 are in qualitative agreement with the expectation that pH effects slow down vertical growth in later stages.
source: Our observations shown in Figure 1H and Figure 1—figure supplement 1 are in qualitative agreement with the expectation.
evidence: This compares experimental observations to model predictions.

claim: Recent series of colony-based microbial range expansion studies, which involve much larger colony sizes and longer periods of colony growth, are likely in the late regime where vertical growth has ceased.
source: Note that recent series of colony-based microbial range expansion studies (Hallatschek et al., 2007; Hallatschek and Nelson, 2010; Korolev et al., 2012), which involve much larger colony sizes and longer periods of colony growth, are likely in this late regime where vertical growth has ceased.
evidence: This is an inference about other studies with citations.

claim: The radial expansion of large colonies in range expansion studies may still be governed by the same factors discussed in this work.
source: Nevertheless, the radial expansion of these large colonies may still be governed by the same factors discussed in this work.
evidence: This is a speculation about the applicability of the model to other studies.

claim: The work establishes that the radial growth of colonies is not limited by nutrient as commonly believed, but by the interplay of surface tension and cell-agar friction.
source: First, we establish that the radial growth of our colonies is not limited by nutrient as commonly believed, but by the interplay of surface tension and cell-agar friction (Figure 9).
evidence: This is a key finding from the study shown in Figure 9.

claim: Given that biofilms have typically much lower bacterial densities, nutrient limitation will be even less of a problem for biofilms.
source: Given that biofilms have typically much lower bacterial densities, nutrient limitation will be even less of a problem.
evidence: This is an inference about biofilms based on the findings.

claim: EPS secreted by the bacteria could modify both the surface tension and cell-agar friction to control the radial expansion speed in biofilms.
source: Also, EPS secreted by the bacteria could modify both the surface tension and cell-agar friction to control the radial expansion speed.
evidence: This is a speculation about biofilms based on the model.

claim: Nutrient supply is limiting for the vertical growth of colonies in this study.
source: Second, nutrient supply is limiting for the vertical growth of our colonies (Figure 9AC).
evidence: This is a key finding from the study shown in Figure 9AC.

claim: Nutrient limitation becomes less of a problem for the loosely packed biofilms.
source: This becomes less of a problem for the loosely packed biofilms.
evidence: This is an inference about biofilms based on the findings.

claim: Biofilms are said to form channels in their interior, which would further alleviate the supply of nutrient, thereby allowing for faster vertical expansion.
source: Moreover, biofilms are said to form channels in their interior (Wilking et al., 2013), which would further alleviate the supply of nutrient, thereby allowing for faster vertical expansion.
evidence: This is an inference about biofilms with citation.

claim: Verticalization of cells in the interior, which is important for vertical growth but occurs at rather large colony sizes according to this model, also occurs in biofilms but at much smaller colony sizes.
source: Finally, verticalization of cells in the interior, which is important for vertical growth but occurs at rather large colony sizes according to our model (Figure 4—figure supplement 1), also occurs in biofilms but at much smaller colony sizes (Beroz et al., 2018; Enos-Berlage and McCarter, 2000; Yan et al., 2016).
evidence: This compares the model predictions to observations in biofilms with citations.

claim: While the precise nature of the forces driving verticalization may be different in colonies and biofilms, the underlying origins may be similar — mechanical instability due to in-plane compression resulting from colony expansion and cell-agar friction.
source: While the precise nature of the forces driving verticalization may be different in the two cases, the underlying origins may be similar — mechanical instability due to in-plane compression resulting from colony expansion and cell-agar friction.
evidence: This is an inference comparing the mechanisms in colonies and biofilms.

claim: The additional ingredients provided by biofilms enable the colonies to expand faster both horizontally and vertically.
source: In light of these comparisons, we see that the additional ingredients provided by biofilms enable the colonies to expand faster both horizontally and vertically.
evidence: This is an inference about biofilms based on the comparisons.

claim: The model presented here, with results quantitatively comparable to experimental data, can be used to interpret large-scale data being generated by high-throughput colony growth assays to track the growth of different strains in different conditions.
source: The model presented here, with results quantitatively comparable to experimental data, can be used to interpret large-scale data being generated by high-throughput colony growth assays to track the growth of different strains in different conditions (Takeuchi et al., 2014).
evidence: This describes a potential application of the model with citation.

claim: The model can be used as a launching pad to include more complex effects of metabolism and cell growth, as well as other factors such as extracellular matrix to allow the simulation of biofilms, and multiple interacting species to explore microbial ecology in compact space.
source: Our model can be used as a launching pad, not only to include the more complex effects of metabolism and cell growth mentioned here, but also other factors such as extracellular matrix to allow the simulation of biofilms, and multiple interacting species to explore microbial ecology in compact space.
evidence: This describes potential future extensions of the model.

claim: It will be an interesting challenge to develop coarse-grained hydrodynamic models that incorporate the unique features of surface tension and dynamic friction discussed here, and capture the radial and vertical colony growth characteristics.
source: Finally, it will be an interesting challenge to develop coarse-grained hydrodynamic models that incorporate the unique features of surface tension and dynamic friction discussed here, and capture the radial and vertical colony growth characteristics, both their temporal behaviors and their dependences on cell growth rates and other environmental factors.
evidence: This describes a future research direction.

claim: The strain of E. coli K12 used in all the experiments, EQ59, was derived from NCM3722.
source: The strain of E. coli K12 used in all the experiments reported in this work, EQ59, was derived from NCM3722 (Lyons et al., 2011), with deletion of the motA gene to remove bacterial motility and harboring constitutive GFP expression.
evidence: This describes the bacterial strain used with citation.

claim: Biofilm formation is highly suppressed in NCM3722, as acquired nonsense mutations within both the bsg and csg operons prevent the synthesis of extracellular cellulose and curli needed to support biofilm.
source: We note that biofilm formation is highly suppressed in NCM3722, as acquired nonsense mutations within both the bsg and csg operons prevent the synthesis of extracellular cellulose and curli needed to support biofilm (Lyons et al., 2011; Serra et al., 2013).
evidence: This describes a property of the strain with citations.

claim: The model uses static and dynamic friction as described in models of granular solids.
source: In our model, we found it necessary to further include static and dynamic friction as described below.
evidence: This describes the friction model used.

claim: The model follows standard models of granular solids, first introduced to cell modeling by Tsimring and his collaborators.
source: We follow standard models of granular solids (Brilliantov et al., 1996; Cundall and Strack, 1979; Kuwabara and Kono, 1987; Shäfer et al., 1996), first introduced to cell modeling by Tsimring and his collaborators (Volfson et al., 2008).
evidence: This cites the origin of the friction model used.

claim: A dynamic friction form imposed by Equation 7b provides a natural explanation of the experimental observation that the radial velocity of the colony is independent of the cell growth rate.
source: As we see in 'Radial expansion – quantitative analysis', a dynamic friction form imposed by Equation 7b provides a natural explanation of the experimental observation that the radial velocity of the colony is independent of the cell growth rate.
evidence: This describes the importance of the dynamic friction model.

claim: In high-density colonies such as those studied here, dissipation due to viscous drag is significantly less than the cellular friction force.
source: We note that in high-density colonies such as those studied here, dissipation due to viscous drag is significantly less than the cellular friction force.
evidence: This is an assessment of the relative importance of different forces.

claim: Surface tension is frequently treated as a property of a composite fluid comprising of cells plus the surrounding fluid.
source: It is frequently treated as a property of a composite fluid comprising of cells plus the surrounding fluid (Grimson and Barker, 1993; Zhang et al., 2008).
evidence: This cites common approaches to modeling surface tension.

claim: Alternatively, the liquid phase is ignored altogether, and surface tension is assumed to arise from attractive interactions between the cells themselves.
source: Alternatively, the liquid phase is ignored altogether, and surface tension is assumed to arise from attractive interactions between the cells themselves (Ben-Jacob et al., 2000).
evidence: This cites an alternative approach to modeling surface tension.

claim: Coarse-grained treatments of surface tension cannot describe the initial layer-by-layer growth of the colony arising from buckling, nor can they capture thin layers surrounding the periphery of large colonies.
source: However, such coarse-grained treatments of surface tension cannot describe the initial layer-by-layer growth of the colony arising from buckling (Figure 1A–E), nor can they capture thin layers surrounding the periphery of large colonies (Figure 14).
evidence: This critiques prior approaches to modeling surface tension.

claim: Surface tension is modeled as a boundary force experienced by discrete cells at the colony boundary due to increased surface tension of the continuum liquid these cells are immersed in.
source: In order to capture these effects, we endeavor here to model the surface tension experienced by cells in a colony as a boundary force, that is as force experienced by discrete cells at the colony boundary due to increased surface tension of the continuum liquid these cells are immersed in.
evidence: This describes the novel surface tension model.

claim: For E. coli growing on hard agar, the cells themselves have no appreciable attraction to one another.
source: For E. coli growing on hard agar, the cells themselves have no appreciable attraction to one another.
evidence: This is an assumption about cell-cell interactions.

claim: Cells are held together at high densities in a colony above the agar through the surrounding liquid they share.
source: They are instead held together at high densities in a colony above the agar through the surrounding liquid they share (blue color in Figure 14A): Liquid is pulled into and retained in the colony through the osmotic effects of hydrophilic molecules on cell surface (Seminara et al., 2012), wetting the surface of cells in the colony including those at the boundary.
evidence: This describes the mechanism of cell cohesion with citation.

claim: The cellular density within the colony is determined by the osmotic balance between the colony and the agar.
source: One can think of the cellular density within the colony as determined by the osmotic balance between the colony and the agar.
evidence: This is an inference about cellular density.

claim: Colonies grown on lower density agar are more liquid-like.
source: This can be readily observed, as colonies grown on lower density agar are more liquid-like.
evidence: This is an experimental observation.

claim: This large cell-level surface tension is able to hold a large group of cells in a monolayer above the agar surface, until the pressure inside the expanding monolayer exceeds a critical level to overcome the liquid surface tension resisting vertical protrusion, resulting in the 'buckling' of the monolayer into multiple layers.
source: As shown in 'Radial expansion – quantitative analysis' and illustrated in Figure 14B, this large cell-level surface tension is able to hold a large group of cells in a monolayer above the agar surface, until the pressure inside the expanding monolayer (due to friction against motion on agar surface) exceeds a critical level to overcome the liquid surface tension resisting vertical protrusion, resulting in the 'buckling' of the monolayer into multiple layers.
evidence: This describes the role of surface tension in buckling.

claim: The velocity Verlet algorithm, a commonly used molecular dynamics simulations of macromolecules, is used to update the cell velocities and positions.
source: We use the velocity Verlet algorithm, a commonly used molecular dynamics simulations of macromolecules, to update the cell velocities and positions (Frenkel and Smit, 2002).
evidence: This describes the numerical algorithm used with citation.

claim: Multi-resolution adaptive grids are used for a large computational domain, and OpenMP is used for parallelizing the code.
source: We use multi-resolution adaptive grids for a large computational domain, and use the OpenMP for parallelizing our code.
evidence: This describes the numerical implementation.

claim: On a multi-processor (14-16 processors) computer, the simulation can reach a colony of a few million cells in 24 hours.
source: On a multi-processor (14-16 processors) computer, the simulation can reach a colony of a few million cells in 24 hours.
evidence: This describes the computational performance.

claim: The major and basic parts of the C++ codes have been placed in the repository GitHub.
source: We have placed the major and basic parts of our C++ codes in the repository GitHub (Warren et al., 2019; copy archived at https://github.com/elifesciences-publications/CellsMD3D).
evidence: This describes the code availability.
